We've seen multiple examples proving that granting Meta's Muse app full disk access on Mac is a terrible idea, and now another serious privacy issue has surfaced. The latest finding is that Muse analyzes your communications with every person in your life every hour.

Apple's concern over this development is justified; the company said in a blog post that it will introduce additional controls for the "full disk access" feature to address the root of the problem...

Meta's Muse app makes the problem urgent

Meta recently launched its personal AI agent app, Muse, for iPhone and Mac. Despite the folly of giving a Meta app unfettered access to everything on your Apple device, the app quickly rose to the top of the App Store charts.

Unsurprisingly, problems came quickly and did not improve afterward — *Wired* reported that security researcher Karan Joshi discovered Meta has instructed Muse to capture all the information needed to build a complete map of all your relationships.

One of Muse's instructions appears to be the ability to "create a dedicated page for every person in the user's life." This hourly process includes organizing information on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "collaborators," and people you "follow." The instructions also state: "where they live, training background, recurring topics (moving, shared savings goals)." The model can also record "important days" such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history log may include background information such as "a March trip, a resolved argument, a milestone last week."

Apple tightens controls on full disk access

You might think the permission prompt that appears when granting an app "full disk access" on Mac is clear enough, but that doesn't seem to be the case. Even tech-savvy users have handed over this unrestricted access without fully understanding how dangerous it is.

Apple said the feature was originally designed for backup apps, but developers have now used it for much more, including AI agents. The company has said it intends to "introduce additional controls" to ensure users fully understand what they're doing when granting this permission.

What Apple must and must not do

Apple considers this move "essential," and I fully agree. When existing permission requests fail to adequately convey the seriousness of what users are agreeing to, Apple has a responsibility to make sure users truly understand what they're allowing.

What I'd like to see is clearer language warning users not to proceed unless they're sure of the consequences. The wording would read roughly as follows:

Basically, warnings cannot be too strong. For apps that have already been granted this permission, I'd also accept a one-time confirmation requirement for users.

Peter's hot takes

Although Apple's occasional asking whether I want to continue letting an app access location data is a bit annoying, I do appreciate it. At least once, I realized I no longer wanted an app to keep that level of access. It also reminds me to think regularly about which apps might still be using my location data.

However, Apple absolutely must not repeat the mistake it made with screen recording in macOS Sequoia. Of course, that feature is also extremely dangerous, so pairing it with the strongest warning is appropriate — but what Apple did at the time was force us to re-confirm these permissions every week and after every reboot.

This approach was widely criticized for turning macOS into Microsoft Vista and imposing on users a "subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel." In my view, the occasional re-confirmation pop-ups Apple currently throws up on iPhone are already too much. For example, I've authorized Citymapper to access my location so it can keep providing navigation in the background, so Apple, I really don't need you asking me again whether I still want to do that.

Yes, issue the strongest possible warning for full disk access, but if someone chooses to proceed, macOS must respect that decision. Please, no weekly or other forced re-confirmation mechanisms.
